content: In 1995, the World Health Organization (WHO) introduced the Global School Health Initiative, aiming to enhance the health of children, adolescents, and communities through Health-Promoting Schools (HPS). Research has shown that HPS can effectively improve various aspects of student health. However, achieving widespread, high-quality, and sustainable implementation of these programs has been challenging in many countries. Collaboration between the education and health sectors, as well as other stakeholders, is essential for the success of HPS. This interdisciplinary approach is particularly critical for school health services (SHS), which require medical expertise and coordination at all levels of the system. Recently, WHO, UNESCO, and other United Nations partners launched the Making Every School a Health-Promoting School initiative. This initiative aims to strengthen the education sector's ability to integrate health and well-being considerations into schools using a whole-school approach. As part of this effort, global standards for HPS have been established, including a requirement for access to comprehensive school-based or school-linked health services. These services address students' physical, emotional, psychosocial, and educational health needs. The WHO guideline on SHS provides national governments and stakeholders with detailed recommendations on the effectiveness, acceptability, and content of comprehensive SHS involving health workers. The guideline development was guided by three key questions: (1) Are comprehensive SHS effective in improving health outcomes or increasing health service coverage for school-aged children and adolescents, including cost-effectiveness? (2) Are these services acceptable to stakeholders such as students, parents, teachers, and policymakers? (3) What should the content of comprehensive SHS be in different contexts? The primary audience for this guideline includes government policymakers, program managers, and private stakeholders in the health and education sectors responsible for the health and well-being of school-aged children (5–19 years). The guideline can be used to develop and improve SHS policies and programs. It emphasizes the importance of implementing comprehensive SHS and provides evidence-based recommendations to support these efforts. Additionally, it offers a menu of interventions and supporting evidence to guide the selection of SHS interventions at the national level. The guideline outlines 87 interventions categorized by health area, type of health activity, and their suitability for inclusion in SHS.g., immunizations), clinical assessments, and support for other pillars of health-promoting schools. Examples include promoting health literacy, conducting routine preventive health check-ups, providing first aid, and supporting mental health and substance use interventions. The development of this guideline followed WHO's standard procedures and involved an independent Guideline Development Group (GDG) with diverse representation. The GDG reviewed global WHO guidance documents, conducted expert surveys, and prioritized interventions based on their relevance and suitability for SHS. The final list of 87 interventions was categorized as essential or suitable for inclusion in SHS, either universally or in specific geographic areas. The guideline also highlights the global burden of disease among school-aged children and adolescents. Despite significant progress in reducing mortality rates and improving nutrition, substantial health challenges persist, including unintentional injuries, interpersonal violence, sexual and reproductive health issues, communicable and non-communicable diseases, and mental health concerns. Road injuries, lower respiratory infections, and diarrheal diseases remain leading causes of death, while conditions such as iron-deficiency anemia, anxiety disorders, and asthma contribute significantly to years lived with disability (YLD). Certain subpopulations of children and adolescents are particularly vulnerable, facing higher health risks, limited access to services, and worse health outcomes. Addressing these disparities requires targeted interventions that address the social determinants of health. Improving the quality, coverage, and equity of SHS can contribute to achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as ensuring healthy lives (SDG 3), achieving gender equality (SDG 5), and reducing inequalities (SDG 10). In addition to addressing health problems, SHS should focus on promoting positive health and well-being, supporting healthy transitions, and fostering skills and behaviors that enable children and adolescents to navigate their environments effectively. This includes health education on topics like nutrition, physical activity, and reproductive health, as well as participatory activities that promote well-being and health-seeking behaviors. By addressing both health challenges and positive development, SHS can play a critical role in supporting the overall growth and success of school-aged children and adolescents.
